Through her work, Somers reimagines everyday life and explores what she terms the "subtle treason of objects." Employing a distinct visual language characterized by a sense of play, bright colours, a mocking tone, and exaggerated shapes, she actively challenges prevailing ideas of normalcy, beauty, and refinement.Her sculptures serve as a powerful critique of the Christian-Colonial gaze that remains fixed upon southern Africa. Somers' work is held in numerous private and public collections, including the prestigious Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

item.title: Xavier Briel
item.description: Xavier Briel, born and raised in Pretoria, moved to Cape Town in 2010, inspired by its stunning landscapes. Initially a draughtsman and IT professional, he discovered his passion for photography while exploring South Africa’s outdoors. In 2016, Xavier left his job to pursue photography full-time, focusing on capturing the raw energy of adventure sports, especially trail running.His big break came when his work at PUFfeR 2016 led to opportunities with Ultra-Trail Cape Town and other major events. Known for his ability to run long distances with a camera, Xavier’s work is defined by his belief that great stories come from pushing beyond comfort zones.With dreams of shooting in Africa’s most remote locations, Xavier aims to link adventure photography with conservation, showcasing the continent’s beauty and challenges through his lens. Inspired by local talents like Kelvin Trautman and Craig Kolesky, he continues to push his creative and physical boundaries.

item.title: Xoliswa Ngwenya
item.description: Xoliswa Ngwenya is a Johannesburg-based visual artist, photographer, and archivist whose work is deeply engaged with social and historical narratives. An alumnus of the renowned Market Photo Workshop and a current BA student at Unisa, Ngwenya has built a career distinguished by prestigious accolades and significant contributions to the archival field.Her impactful photography has earned her numerous awards. In 2025, she was named a runner-up for the esteemed Tierney Fellowship. Her previous honours include winning first prize in the social justice photography competition from the Open Society Foundation for South Africa (2016), being shortlisted for the DemocraSEE 3 award (2018), the Magnum Foundation Fellowship (2019), and the Contemporary African Photography (CAP) Prize (2019). Most recently, she was a finalist for the Ilford Photo Community Grant (2024) and has been nominated for World Press Photo’s prestigious 2025 Joop Swart Masterclass.Beyond her personal practice, Ngwenya is a respected educator and archivist. She has facilitated digital curation and digitisation training at the University of Johannesburg, Wits University, and Bailey’s African History Archive. Her archival expertise has been instrumental in preserving the legacies of iconic photographers, having worked on the archives of David Goldblatt, Ruth Motau, and Ernest Cole.

item.title: Xolelwa Malinga "XO"
item.description: Xolelwa Malinga, also known as XO, is a self-taught multidisciplinary artist born and raised in the Kingdom of Eswatini. Her work is a focused and powerful exploration of the female form, using the anatomy as a canvas to convey nuanced feelings, thoughts, and complex themes.Inspired by the subtle communication of body positioning, XO’s art delves into concepts of beauty, freedom, and confidence. Her primary aim is to celebrate the vibrant essence of women and to inspire a profound sense of self-acceptance.Beyond celebration, her work serves a critical purpose: to actively challenge and dismantle societal norms that lead to the objectification of the black female figure. By creating art that honours and appreciates its subject, she directly confronts the pervasive sexualization perpetuated by the legacies of colonialism and modern media, advocating for a new perspective.

item.title: Yakno Abasi Ene
item.description: Yakno-Abasi Ene is an abstract realism artist based in Lagos Nigeria.Yakno-Abasi's artistic journey, delves into the profound realms of sisterhood, women's empowerment, and the divine feminine. Shaped by the nurturing bonds within my predominantly female family, her work aims to illuminate the varied roles of women and address the challenges they navigate. Each creation is a testament to her idealistic vision of societal development, capturing the essence of unity and strength inherent in sisterhood. Empowerment, a recurring theme, resonates through her art, advocating for the elevation of women in all facets of life.The divine feminine, a source of inspiration, lends a spiritual and transcendent dimension to her work, celebrating the inherent grace and power within every woman. Through diverse mediums, her art mirrors the dynamic interplay of surroundings, personal experiences, and an ever-evolving imagination. As I navigate this continuous learning journey as an emerging artist, her central goal remains to educate, heal, and inspire, contributing to a more inclusive and equitable world by spotlighting the beauty and resilience of women.

item.title: Yannis Davy Guibinga
item.description: Yannis Davy Guibinga (b.1995) is a celebrated photographer and master storyteller from Libreville, Gabon. His work is a vibrant and essential exploration of the diverse identities and cultures found across Africa and its global diaspora.Guibinga uses his lens not merely to document but to celebrate this rich multiplicity. His primary mission is to actively counter the singular, often reductive narratives that have historically been associated with the African continent. Through a powerful combination of narrative depth and an incisive eye for composition and colour, he creates images that are both visually stunning and conceptually profound.This unique and compelling vision has enabled Guibinga to build an extensive and remarkable portfolio, leading to prestigious collaborations with world-renowned brands such as Apple and Nikon, solidifying his status as a significant voice in contemporary photography.

item.title: Yinkore
item.description: Yinkore (b. 1998) is a self-taught Nigerian digital artist currently based in Canada. Her work is a powerful exploration of intersectionality and representation, born from her unique lived experiences.As a dark-skinned black bisexual woman, Yinkore is keenly aware of the rarity of seeing stories like hers told authentically. She uses her art as a form of activism and a voice to resist the silence often imposed upon individuals with multiple minority statuses.Through her digital creations, she navigates complex themes and advocates for the portrayal of every possible identity within the evolving landscape of contemporary art. Her work stands as a defiant and necessary testament to the importance of being seen and heard.

item.title: Yolanda Mazwana
item.description: Yolanda Mazwana (b. 1996, Eastern Cape) is a Johannesburg-based, self-taught visual artist whose paintings investigates themes surrounding mental health, the female body, and cultural identity. Mazwana synthesizes elements of abstract expressionism, neo-expressionism, and symbolism to explore the complexities of inner experience, trauma, and personal resilience.Through layered textures, bold colours and distorted forms, her figures become symbolic reflections of societal pressures, emotional vulnerabilities, probing questions of selfhood. Mazwana's recent solo exhibitions, Symptoms of Nothing at Kalashnikovv Gallery and Secret Homegirls at Daville Baillie Gallery (both in 2019), delve into subjects such as anxiety, isolation, and subconscious. Her work often portrays characters and symbols representing agoraphobia, hypochondria, and inner conflict, transforming these themes into vibrant narratives that resonate with the viewer's shared experiences. Her art has been showcased in numerous group exhibitions and major art fairs, including the Investec Cape Town Art Fair, FNB Art Joburg Fair, and RMB Turbine Art Fair. In recognition of her contributions of contemporary art, Mazwana received The Bag Factory Young Woman Studio Bursary in 2019 and secured the second prize for the Emerging Painting Invitational Prize in 2020.

item.title: Yonela Makoba
item.description: Yonela Makoba (b. 1993, Eastern Cape, South Africa) is a transdisciplinary artist, cultural worker, and researcher working across performance, installation, photography, printmaking, and text. Rooted in Indigenous knowledge systems, their practice moves through memory, ritual, and the knowledge carried by black bodies.Drawing on autoethnography, Indigenous knowledge, Pan-Africanism, and Black feminist thought, Makoba works with movement, fabric, natural materials, and voice to explore the relationality between spirits, people, and things. Guided by the Xhosa axiom uhamba kubona (to go is to see), and what they term ukulu(o)ngu(o)za, their work embraces wandering and phenomenology as methodologies for coming into knowledge (ancestral and otherwise), and for intuitively composing rituals, gatherings, and happenings for the present.Central to their practice is iTi, a Xhosa ritual of remembering matriarchal ancestors, which they have been critically and intuitively fabulating through an ongoing series titled iTi Ritual Studies. These iterations experiment with holding space for multiple permutations of the ritual, exploring its shifts, silences, and possibilities across time and space. Through this work, Makoba is developing a language and practice for creating and holding ritual space in various media. Makoba holds a Master’s degree in Theatre and Performance and a BSc in Environmental and Geographic Science from the University of Cape Town. Their work has been presented in solo and group exhibitions, performances, and art fairs, including the recent solo presentation Rooi-land (Red-land) at Suidoosterfees at Artscape in early 2026, and the group exhibition I Keep Coming Back, I Don’t Know Why at Stevenson Gallery. Makoba will be featured in Iziko Museums’ Materiality V2, opening late August 2026, and in the 15th edition of the Rencontres de Bamako nov 2026-jan 2027.

item.title: Yusuf Durodola
item.description: Durodola Yusuf (b. 1979) is a distinguished Nigerian painter and performance artist known for his innovative use of recycled waste materials. Born in Ibadan, Oyo State, Yusuf holds an NCE from the Federal College of Education, Akoka, and a Bachelor of Arts in Fine Arts from the University of Lagos.His work confronts pressing socio-cultural issues, including social justice, environmental pollution, and the complexities of the human experience. A passionate advocate for environmentalism, Yusuf often engages the public directly through thought-provoking performance art. His pieces, such as the notable ‘Global Hues’, are a powerful call for collective action, underscored by his belief that "we are the change the world is earnestly awaiting."Deeply rooted in his heritage, Yusuf draws inspiration from traditional Yoruba idioms, proverbs, and adages, which lend sincerity and cultural authenticity to his work. This focus on his cultural identity is evident not only in the Yoruba themes of his performances but also in the distinct patterns and material choices within his paintings and experimental art. Through his dynamic practice, Yusuf skillfully merges tradition with contemporary commentary, creating work that is both culturally specific and universally resonant.

item.title: Zacharaha Magasa
item.description: Zacharaha Magasa (b. 1988) is a Zimbabwean artist who creates work driven by the direct and indirect dialogues of everyday life. Their practice is a profound investigation into socio-politics, environmental decay, and themes of territorial and cultural resistance.Drawing inspiration from their immediate surroundings—from politically charged gatherings to the pervasive systems of consumerism—the artist explores how language and communication convey complex messages, whether about climate change or police brutality. The choice of materials is central to their work, with non-conventional items selected for their potent symbolism. Rubber is a prevalent medium, deliberately used for its powerful association with the histories of slavery and oppression in Africa and across the globe.Stylistically, the work is characterized by the use of lines to create figurative and symbolic forms. These lines suggest movement, drifting between figuration and abstraction, and referencing both contemporary political events and personal childhood memories. Techniques like weaving rubber strips speak directly to Zimbabwean traditions and the ideal of unity. By manipulating materials like rubber or telephone lines, the artist explores how meaning is constructed and carried, creating a multi-layered and critical commentary on the world.

item.title: Zac Zinn
item.description: Zac Zinn is a BCom Digital Marketing graduate currently working as a Photographer, Videographer, and Designer for ES Media. His passion for photography has taken him to unexpected places and given him a unique perspective on life, instilling a deep appreciation for the subtle, intricate details of the world around him.Zac's creative journey has also led him to excel in social media management, where he enjoys crafting meaningful connections and engaging with diverse digital audiences. Highly skilled across the Adobe Creative Suite, he seamlessly combines his technical expertise in photography, videography, and graphic design to create compelling, high-impact visual content. Driven by curiosity and a commitment to continuous growth, his work constantly fuels his passion for capturing stories, environments, and moments in fresh, visually inspiring ways.

item.title: Zama Spellman
item.description: Zama Spellman (b. 1999) is a visual artist based in Gqeberha, Eastern Cape, whose work is a compelling exploration of black femininity. A graduate of Nelson Mandela University with a Bachelor of Visual Arts, she is currently pursuing her Honours degree in Fine Art at the same institution.Spellman's practice delves into critical themes of race, representation, and displacement. She primarily works in oil painting to create rich and bold portraiture, alongside detailed charcoal drawings that place black women in their intimate spaces. Through her chosen media, she captures the nuanced experiences and powerful presence of her subjects.Her emerging career has already been marked by significant achievements. In 2021, she was selected as a finalist for the prestigious Sasol New Signatures art competition. Her work has been featured in notable group exhibitions, including "Same size, Same price, No signature" at Art on Target and "Learning from our context: Revitalising and Decolonising the Visual and Performing Arts" at Nelson Mandela University.

item.title: Zamani Xaba
item.description: Zamani Xaba, born in eThekwini, KwaZulu-Natal, is an artist whose work is a powerful commentary on heritage, labour, and socio-economic inequality in South Africa. His formal artistic journey began with classes at the Durban Institute of Technology and led to a diploma from Ekurhuleni East College. He further honed his skills as a printmaker, graduating from the prestigious Artist Proof Studio in 2016.In his latest body of work, the ‘Naked Tailor Series’, Xaba uses the sewing machine as a profound and multi-layered symbol. This motif is deeply rooted in his personal history, representing his family's lineage of seamstresses, upholsterers, and tailors. However, the symbol transcends personal heritage to ask a critical question: when does the representation of an object become more than the object itself?The series features an anonymous, silhouetted figure struggling under the immense weight of a sewing machine, reminiscent of Atlas carrying the globe. Here, the weight is the crushing pressure of unseen economic and social forces. The tailor is depicted naked because he is unable to afford the very clothes he creates—a poignant critique of the vast gap between the rich and the poor. Through these works, Xaba gives form to an unseen populace smothered under the force of systemic pressure, creating a moving personification of struggle and resilience.

item.title: Zander Blom
item.description: Zander Blom (b. 1982, Pretoria) is a prominent South African contemporary artist celebrated for his dynamic and experimental approach to painting. Initially enrolling in Information Design, Blom soon left formal studies to independently pursue his passion for art, beginning with printmaking and video before dedicating himself to painting. Now based in Cape Town, he has become a significant figure in the global art scene.Deeply influenced by 20th-century modernism, Blom’s work engages in a vigorous dialogue with art history, referencing masters like Mondrian and Bacon while constantly challenging the conventions of painting. His practice is characterized by a relentless drive for innovation, not only in composition but also in method. He famously repurposes everyday objects into unconventional tools, creating richly textured and gestural impasto works on unprimed Belgian linen.Blom’s career has moved through distinct phases, from early photographic projects documenting installations in his studio to various styles of abstraction and a recent return to monochrome palettes. This constant evolution is central to his process, which he views as a "voyage of discovery."He has held numerous solo exhibitions at leading galleries, including STEVENSON in Cape Town and Johannesburg, and Galerie Hans Mayer in Düsseldorf. His work has been featured in major institutions such as the Norval Foundation and the Iziko South African National Gallery. In 2014, Blom won the prestigious Jean-François Prat Prize in Paris, and his work is included in Phaidon's seminal anthology, Vitamin P3: New Perspectives in Painting.

item.title: Zandri Oosthuysen
item.description: Zandri Oosthuysen's work is a profound exploration of mortality and death, deeply rooted in the historical tradition of memento mori—the Latin reminder that 'you will die'. Drawing inspiration from the Vanitas still life genre prevalent during the Baroque period, she reinterprets its core themes for a contemporary context.Instead of traditional symbols like human skulls, Oosthuysen uses animal remains—skulls, flesh, and bones—as the central subjects of her work. This fascination stems from a deeply personal place of processing her own mortality. Through the repetitive and meticulous study of these decaying forms, she creates powerful still lifes that serve as a contemplation on the transience of life.The decaying animal remains act as a direct mirror to our own human condition, reminding the viewer that we, too, are flesh and bones destined for the same fate. Through this process, Oosthuysen confronts the finality of death and the profound significance of what 'remains'—the lifeless forms that were once associated with life.

item.title: Zanele Montle
item.description: Zanele Montle explores the profound anxieties of migration and the journey of creating a home away from home. Drawing from her own experience of moving from Kwa-Zulu Natal to the city, her work is a deeply personal investigation of adaptation and identity.Her primary subject matter is derived from old family photographs, with a particular focus on her mother and siblings. These figures are brought to the forefront through the use of vibrant, bright backgrounds that make them prominent and immediate. In a deliberate effort to remain connected to her roots, she titles each work in isiZulu, evoking a powerful sense of nostalgia, community, and personal history.Zanele holds a National Diploma in Visual Art from the University of Johannesburg and a postgraduate qualification in art education. Her talent was recognized early when she became a finalist in the Thami Mnyele Fine Art Competition in 2015. After gaining industry experience as a gallery manager, she now dedicates her time to her dual practice as an arts educator and a painter. In 2021, she was honoured as the recipient of the inaugural META Foundation 'Womxn to Watch' Award.

item.title: Zhané Warren
item.description: Zhané Warren (b. 1976, Johannesburg), is the master printer and director at Warren Editions, a printmaking studio based in Cape Town. She studied Fine Art at Stellenbosch University and earned a master’s degree in Technology of Fine Art from the University of Johannesburg in 2006. Awarded a scholarship, she attended the Karel de Grote Hogeskool in Antwerp, Belgium, where she spent five years working alongside renowned artists and printmakers.In 2007, Zhané returned to South Africa as a recognized master printer and founded Warren Editions. As both a visual and performance artist, she has staged numerous exhibitions and performances in South Africa and internationally. Her solo exhibitions include "Live with me" (KZN Gallery, Durban, 2007), "Recurrence" (Art on Paper, Johannesburg, 2006), and "In between here and there" (with Robert van Dromme at Contemporary Wei, Antwerp, Belgium). Her work is represented in various collections in South Africa, Belgium, and the USA.Zhané Warren is also a respected authority in printmaking and fine art publishing, and she is a passionate educator.

item.title: Zolile Phetshane
item.description: Zolile Phetshane (b. 1973) is a prominent South African artist whose work delves into complex contemporary themes such as religion, politics, consumerism, and capitalism. He holds an Advanced Diploma in Fine Arts from the University of the Witwatersrand (2006) and further honed his skills at the renowned Artist Proof Studios in Johannesburg.Phetshane’s distinctive style masterfully combines abstract colour fields with figurative elements and symbols to explore the intricacies of his chosen subjects. He is a versatile artist, working across a range of mediums including printmaking, works on paper in pastel, and acrylic and oil on canvas.Since 2008, he has developed a close and enduring partnership with Lizamore & Associates, leading to significant visibility and success. Through the gallery, he has participated in major art fairs like the FNB Joburg Art Fair, Investec Cape Town Art Fair, and the RMB Turbine Art Fair. He has also held several successful solo exhibitions with the gallery, including "1 is the magic number" (2016), "Simplified Complexity" (2018), and "Neon Paradise" (2020), the latter being a collaboration with artist Anton Burger.Phetshane's work has also been exhibited at institutions like the North West University Gallery (2014) and internationally with Clifton Boulder in Europe. Highly sought after by collectors, his art is featured in numerous prominent private and public collections.

item.title: Bolelang Leepile
item.description: Bolelang Leepile (b. 1992, Dobsonville Gardens, Soweto) is a South African artist, printmaker, and freelance curator. Working primarily in linocut and other printmaking techniques, Leepile explores themes rooted in personal and collective narratives. He maintains an active studio practice while also engaging in curatorial work across South Africa’s dynamic art scene.Leepile has served as a curatorial assistant for projects at notable platforms such as the Turbine Art Fair, FNB Art Joburg, and Gallery Noko. His work has been included in numerous group exhibitions and is available for sale and rental through Saatchi Art and The Art Bank of South Africa.

item.title: Bonginkosi Mavuso
item.description: Bonginkosi Thato Mavuso was born in 1988 in Pimville, Soweto. In 2007 he received his Diploma in Graphics & Animation, in Parktown College Campus and the following year a BA in Visual Arts & Printmaking at University of Johannesburg. He's preferred style is Abstract-Expressionism and Portraiture with the usage of mixed media to execute his work. Mavuso has been included in the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) Call for Creatives for raising awareness for the Covid-19 Pandemic. In 2017 Bonginkosi was a resident artist at BOCOMO ART CENTER where he offered art lessons and art related community projects in and around Kliptown.Currently the artist is working with Soweto Kliptown Youth (SKY) engaging in artistic programs with children. Mavuso's work can also be seen on walls/murals in and around Soweto and Johannesburg in which he has collaborated with several artists of his caliber, Graphic and Fine artist's alike. His numerous group exhibitions include Joburg Fringe, panel selected group exhibition, The Art Room, Jhb, and Turbine Art Fair, Gallery 2, Jhb. He is one of the founders of MAKEBA Designs & Collectables (PTY) Ltd in 2021 in partnership with Kebaabetswe Letau who's a wood worker and designer. He is currently working on a series of paintings for the Nyrox Sculpture Park late 2021, and a collaborative exhibition in Zollikon, Switzerland which is part of a 6 month residency program.

item.title: Buntu Qina
item.description: Buntu Qina is a multifaceted artist whose creative passions span a diverse range of mediums, from the rich depths of charcoal and graphite to the vibrant hues of acrylics and oils. With an unwavering dedication to his craft, Qina's artistic prowess shines through in his captivating portraits, as well as his exploration of landscapes, seascapes, cityscapes, and still life compositions.At the heart of Qina's artistic practice is a deep reverence for his people and the way in which light interacts with his subject matter. His keen eye for observation and his ability to capture the essence of his subjects have earned him widespread acclaim, as he consistently produces works that resonate profoundly with viewers.

item.title: Deidre Howarth
item.description: Deidre is an avid visual artist with a profound, lifelong passion for oil on canvas and board painting. Deeply inspired by the masterly techniques of renowned English landscape painters, she explores bold, expansive brushstrokes to capture the core essence and living spirit of her subjects. Her artistic language balances classical influence with modern execution, breathing fresh energy into traditional themes.As an impressionist at heart with a distinct romantic touch, Deidre skillfully utilizes palette knives to sculpt heavy layers of paint directly onto the surface. This technique allows her to evoke intricate details, rich textures, and dancing light without overworking the media. By carefully playing with contrasting colours, subtle gradients, and soft shades, she masterfully creates evocative moods and three-dimensional depth that draw viewers into her pieces. Her fluid artistic journey encompasses an exceptionally diverse range of subjects. From breathtaking landscapes and turbulent seascapes to captivating wildlife portraiture and emotional abstract pieces, her portfolio beautifully showcases her extensive technical versatility, vivid imagination, and limitless creativity.

item.title: Felix Shumba
item.description: Felix Shumba (b. 1989, Bulawayo) lives and works in Masvingo, Zimbabwe.Recent exhibitions include: For want of a horse, a button was lost, Tiwani Contemporary, London, UK; Iwillmedievalfutureyou2, Lilith Performance studio, Malmö, Sweden (both 2025); a following year, Galleria Fonti, Naples, Italy; I Dream I’m Crossing the River, Uitstalling gallery, Belgium; Felix Shumba and Martin Seeds: Nervous Lines, Koop Projects, Brighton, UK (both 2024); Felix Shumba and Kiluanji Kia Henda: Memories of a Poisoned River, Museum of Natural History and Jahmek Contemporary Art, Luanda, Angola; Sharjah Biennial 15: Thinking Historically In the Present, Sharjah Art Foundation (all 2023); A Prelude, Bkhz Gallery, Johannesburg (2022).Felix has participated in residencies at International Studio & Curatorial Program (ISCP), New York, USA (2025); Kiluanji Kia Henda Studio / Jahmek Contemporary Art, Luanda, Angola; Edition Verso, Johannesburg, South Africa (both 2023); Sharjah Art Foundation, Sharjah, UAE; Kemang Wa Lehulere Studio: Guest Artist, Cape Town, South Africa (both 2022).Shumba explores social trauma in an attempt to interrogate the ways in which history is constructed. During his residency at the edition ~ verso studio, Shumba made a series of line etchings titled, The Outsider. Each work, draws from his broader practice at deconstructing spaces (real or imagined)—which he describes as Fold Fields Space (FFS). These are sites generally characterized and haunted by death, trauma, tension, restraint, psychic terror, ecological damage and use of the military as an apparatus of control.Shumba uses art as a mode of revealing the historical masks of violence and their bearing on material realities of blackness, central to Shumba’s work is constant search, probing and questioning of what is at stake, what is hidden, and what trumps the possibility of freedom. The series of etchings in The Outsider unravel a poetic narrative of representation, such as masking and concealment. Shumba engages the illusory, if performative, rituals of power that have sustained regimes of racial capitalist extraction. By deploying a dystopian imagery of the postcolony—culled from archival and media sources on settler-colonial Rhodesia—FFS brings the viewer closer to understanding contemporary predicaments in Zimbabwe.

item.title: Gabrielle Goliath
item.description: Gabrielle Goliath (b.1983) lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. Through the ritual, sonic and social encounters of her practice, Gabrielle Goliath attends (and tends) to histories and present-day conditions of differentially valued life, reaffirming ways in which black, brown, femme and queer practices perform the world differently. Her work troubles a racial/sexual regime of representation, calling for meetings in and across difference, on terms of complicity, relation and love.She has received several awards, including the Future Generation Art Prize – Special Prize (2019), Standard Bank Young Artist Award (2019), and Institut Français, Afrique en créations Prize at the Bamako Biennale (2017). Her work is held in collections such as MoMA, Tate Modern, Kunsthalle Zürich, Mudam Luxembourg, Frac Bretagne, and Iziko South African National Gallery. She lives and works in Johannesburg.

item.title: Gareth Nyandoro
item.description: Gareth Nyandoro was born in 1982 in Bikita, Zimbabwe and currently lives and works in Harare, Zimbabwe Gareth is known for his large works on paper, which often spill out of their two-dimensional frame and into installations including paper scraps and objects found in the markets of Harare, where he is based.The main source of inspiration for Nyandoro’s work is the local markets of Harare, with their buzzing stalls, loud hawkers, frenzied buyers and enticing displays of goods. A keen observer of human behaviour, Nyandoro admires the everyday artistry involved in the displays, where colour, shape, desirability and price all contribute to the competition for the most attractive - and best-selling - stall. His interest in objects and commerce translates into the manifest materiality of his work, but also into its iconography, as he closes in on details from the marketplace: a single shoe here, a hanging shirt there, a batch of designer sunglasses, a lollipop.Nyandoro prepares the various elements of his compositions separately, before assembling them on large sheets of canvas. The result is a collaged aesthetic, suggesting the makeshift appearance of the market. The work is at times abstract, with discarnate human figures barely visible, submerged by grids of inky scratches and checkered patterns: a reflection on the ephemeral, transitional nature of the marketplace and its main actors, rendered through portrayals of everyday experience.The artist's unique technique was inspired by his training as a printmaker: upon preparing an etching, Nyandoro realised he was equally as interested in the engraved copper plate as he was in the print. He thus developed a distinctive working method, derived from etching: using sharp blades, he cut-draws into large pieces of paper and sponges ink onto the surface before removing the top layer of paper with tape.

item.title: Graeme Black
item.description: Born and raised in Angus, Black graduated from the Edinburgh College of Art in 1989 before heading south to pursue his career in pulsating 1990s London. After cutting his teeth working under John Galliano, Arabella Pollen, Zandra Rhodes, he went on to spend 15 years in Italy, working closely with Giorgio Armani on his womenswear collections before becoming Creative Director of womenswear at Salvatore Ferragamo in Florence.Nature, form, colour and texture have been defining elements of Graeme Black’s life and work from his childhood on the rocky east coast of Scotland and his career as an acclaimed international fashion designer, to his current role as a burgeoning artist nestled in the Yorkshire Dales.

item.title: Hlonipani Bhutelezi
item.description: Hloniphani (Mamba) Buthelezi (b. 1990) is a South African multidisciplinary conceptual artist whose creative process spans from using found materials and objects to traditional printmaking and painting. For Buthelezi, art is a channel for making sense of self, ancestry, and the world around him. As part of the 2025 Printmaking Workshop at The Arts Company Soweto, Buthelezi produced new works under the theme 'Reimagining the Next 30 Years' inspired by the 1976 Student uprising in Soweto' in partnership with Constitution Hill and the City of Johannesburg.His recent projects include curating and facilitating the ISIVIVANE Contemporary Art Exhibition (2024), participating in the Durban Art Gallery Group Exhibition (2024), 'Deep in Thought' at virtual Cista Art Gallery in London (2023), His current work is featured in the *Reimagining the Next 30 Years* exhibition at the Women’s Jail at Constitution Hill, and questioning how the youth can shape their future beyond inherited visions. Buthelezi is a multidisciplinary artist who explores cultural memory, spiritual continuity, and socio-political critique through tactile engagement, storytelling, and critical reflection.

item.title: Liz Kobusinge & Darlyne Komukama
item.description: Liz Kobusinge (b. Uganda) is a self-taught artist from Kampala, Uganda, who creates multidisciplinary work exploring mental health and the interior worlds of Black women. Her practice developed as a way to cope with anxiety and depression, positioning art-making as both healing and documentation.Recently, she has been working with handmade bark cloth paper, adapting techniques from Ugandan artist Sheila Nakitende. She views this process as "performance of memory," layering handmade dyes, ink, and video to explore how skin holds and disperses memory. The fragile, degrading materials reflect the ephemeral nature of memory and lived experience, particularly around familial bonds. Kobusinge learned bark cloth papermaking in 2019 during a depressive episode, finding the ritual therapeutic. During her time with the edition ~ verso team, Liz expanded on her paper making practice in deep relation to printmaking and the marks metal retain. Her evolving practice centers on self-hood and autonomy, documenting how people "make peace" as a way to live.Darlyne Komukama (b. Uganda) is a self-taught photographer and multi-media artist who works mostly collaboratively to investigate and edify the things she cares about; femininity, blackness and connectedness. Her feminist ideals are vital to her projects and she will be found working with other women to make some cool shit for even more women to enjoy. Her photographs are full of regal, statuesque Black women, colour and a call back to the natural world.Her visual art projects include; The Salooni, a multi-media roving installation made together with three Ugandan women, investigating and celebrating Black hair, Our Things, a video archive installation made with one other Ugandan woman collecting stories about similar Ugandan experiences, and, Penthouse, a rage room on a rooftop in the middle of downtown Kampala where Kampalan women could safely express and manifest their rage for Kla Art 2018. Her projects, Decay and Cardi Monáe, serve as sonic explorations.As a DJ (Decay), she is interested in feeling and sharing the joy of the power of the femme. Whether she's playing trap, dancehall, ballroom or the stankiest twerking music, it's in service to freedom for the femme body and spirit. With Cardi Monáe, as a producer, she is interested in translating her artistic pursuits, which include photography, videography and installation art, as well as her influences into music.Her work has appeared on CNN, BBC, The Guardian, Quartz and OkayAfrica. Her work has also been shown at the Southbank Centre in London as part of the Africa Utopia Festival, Constitution Hill in Johannesburg as part of the Being Her(e) Exhibition, the Chale Wote Festival in Jamestown in Accra, the Africa Bass Cultural festival in Ouagadougou and at multiple locations in Kampala, Uganda.

item.title: Lizo Pemba
item.description: Lizo Pemba was born at 34 Dubula Street in New Brighton, Port Elizabeth, South Africa. He comes from a rich artistic lineage—his father, Titus Keke Pemba, introduced him to the basics of watercolour painting, while his grandfather, the late Dr. George M.M. Pemba, was a renowned South African artist whose legacy continues to inspire Lizo’s creative path.Lizo began drawing at a young age, developing his skills by copying images from magazines and creating works from imagination. During his school years, he became known as a cartoonist, especially during the turbulent period of political unrest in South Africa.Due to political pressure from the apartheid security forces, Lizo left South Africa and joined Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the African National Congress (ANC), and was based in Angola. While in the military camps, he collaborated with other artists to produce posters, banners, and graphic artworks for the movement. He was later stationed at the ANC printing shop in Luanda, where he created illustrations, political cartoons, and emblems for the ANC and the South African Communist Party (SACP).During his time in Angola, Lizo was commissioned to paint a portrait of SWAPO President Sam Nujoma, which was officially presented by the ANC’s National Executive Committee in Lusaka to the SWAPO leadership. Recognizing his talent, the ANC sent Lizo to Zimbabwe to formally study fine art. Upon returning to South Africa in 1991, he enrolled at the University of Fort Hare in 1992 to pursue a Bachelor of Arts in Fine Arts. Under the mentorship of the late Professor Mike Halier, he excelled in painting, graduating with distinction.While studying, Lizo illustrated books for Lovedale Press and received several private art commissions in Alice and Cape Town. In 1996, he joined the Eastern Cape Department of Sports, Recreation, Arts, and Culture, where he worked to promote visual arts and crafts throughout the region. Lizo has participated in numerous group exhibitions and held two solo exhibitions—one at Highberry Art Gallery, then owned by Cathy Binell, and another in 2009 at the Red Location Museum. In 2005, he was featured in a two-man exhibition at African Feeling Gallery. His work has been profiled in multiple television documentaries, including one in Johnny Clegg’s 'Country Imagine' series.Today, Lizo Pemba continues to use his art to reflect on history, identity, and the enduring spirit of South Africa.

item.title: Lonwabo Yonela Ngcwayi
item.description: Lonwabo Yonela Ngcwayi aims to reveal the subtle nature of power through the moments, spaces, values, and individuals captured in his photographs. His series "Amandla Anobulali" encourages viewers to reassess the ideals they hold in high regard. Ngcwayi invites audiences to explore with him the themes and virtues presented in his work.He emphasizes the inherent strength of traditional Xhosa ways of life and spaces, which are often portrayed and perceived as lesser compared to European standards. His photographs notably showcase imigidi (traditional ceremonies), capturing and exploring the dynamic emotional and somewhat spiritual values reflected in these cultural practices.

item.title: Lookout Sibanda
item.description: Lookout Ceramics, led by a talented artist, is known for their vibrant and textured creations. Inspired by a wide range of sources, from the beauty of nature to the captivating patterns found in fabrics and textiles, Lookout Ceramics infuses their work with a kaleidoscope of colours and intricate textures.The artist behind Lookout Ceramics finds inspiration in the world around them, drawing from the organic shapes and hues found in nature. Additionally, the artist's fascination with fashion and textiles fuels their creative process, leading to the incorporation of captivating patterns into their ceramic pieces. . .

item.title: Lwando Hlazo
item.description: Lwando Hlazo (b. 1994), widely known in creative spaces simply as “Hlazo,” is a Tsolo-born contemporary visual artist and muralist whose practice is characterized by a vibrant, community-driven approach. Deeply rooted in the townships and rural landscapes of the Eastern Cape, his journey is fueled by a desire to uplift and engage the public through visual storytelling. Hlazo holds a BTech degree in Fine Arts from Walter Sisulu University (WSU), an academic foundation that helped him channel post-apartheid socio-economic realities into powerful means of expression. Beyond public walls, his canvas and pencil work—most notably his highly anticipated series Find My Way—utilizes acrylics and intricate charcoal drawings to document daily life, architecture, and heritage within Xhosa communities.

item.title: Mercy Hombakazi Nqandeka
item.description: Mercy Hombakazi Nqandeka is the multi-talented creative force behind Transkei History and Heritage, a collective dedicated to preserving, sharing, and celebrating the rich, complex tapestry of Xhosa culture. Raised in the rural village of Mqhele in Elliotdale along South Africa's Wild Coast, her deep reverence for ancestral traditions, language, and generational storytelling forms the emotional core of her multidisciplinary practice. Nqandeka seamlessly blends evocative visual imagery with carefully crafted written narratives, making her a formidable and passionate contemporary advocate for indigenous knowledge systems.Her artistic and cultural endeavors are backed by an impressive academic foundation. An agriculturalist by training, Nqandeka holds a double Master’s degree in Climate Change, Agriculture, and Transition from the National University of Ireland and SupAgro Montpellier in France, and is currently pursuing a PhD in Health Sciences at Stellenbosch University focusing on indigenous medicine.

item.title: Mziwoxolo Makalima
item.description: Mziwoxolo Makalima is a visual artist whose practice emerges from spontaneous encounters within East London’s communities. Over the years, he has developed a distinctive body of work that investigates the ways of life shaped by collective social movements and everyday struggles.Rather than centering on personal relationships, his approach focuses on observing social interactions in public and communal spaces. This perspective allows him to document the lived realities of oppressed populations and highlight the subtle dynamics that structure their existence.Through this lens, Makalima’s work captures the resilience and spirit of East London communities, serving as both a testimony and a platform for underrepresented voices. His art becomes an act of social documentation, amplifying stories that might otherwise remain unheard.

item.title: Nina Barnett
item.description: Nina Barnett (b. 1983) is a Johannesburg-based artist and researcher. Barnett has worked with edition ~ verso for ten years, including printmaking within her creative practice that uses drawings, immersive installations and experimental filmmaking to engage with questions of geography, infrastructure, materiality, and experiential knowledge. She has recently completed a PhD in Fine Arts from the University of Johannesburg, with a project titled “The Intra-Active Vaal Dam: Imagining Water Beyond the Hydrocolonial”.Barnett’s artistic research regarding water and water systems has recently centred on the re-imagining of Johannesburg’s municipal water beyond the utility, with a focus on the Vaal Dam (the anthropogenic water body that supports the landlocked city) . The cycle of water extraction, purification, pollution and expulsion offers a problematic example of a water as a commodified resource in an era of climate crisis. Barnett’s work brings attention to the materialities of this system and offers alternative ways to know this water through installation, drawing and papermaking.

item.title: Ofentse Motsoane
item.description: Ofentse Motsoane is a dynamic South African artist celebrated for his unique approach to visual storytelling and exploration of cultural identity. Motsoane has emerged as a prominent figure in the contemporary art scene, known for his vibrant and evocative works.Motsoane's art is a reflection of his deep connection to his cultural heritage and his exploration of identity in a rapidly changing world. His compositions often blend traditional motifs with modern elements, creating a rich tapestry that resonates with viewers on multiple levels.Drawing inspiration from the landscapes, traditions, and social dynamics of South Africa, Motsoane's work captures the essence of daily life with a keen eye for detail and a profound sense of storytelling. His paintings and mixed-media pieces exude a sense of energy and emotion, inviting viewers to engage with themes of community, history, and personal journey.

item.title: Sal Price
item.description: Sal Price's artistic creations emerge through a spontaneous dance between intention and serendipity, reflecting the flux of global consciousness. Drawing inspiration from a wide array of influential artists, Price invites viewers to engage in a dialogue that transcends boundaries and sparks imagination.Price's art is a testament to the power of unfettered creativity, where the imagination knows no limits. Each work is a portal into a fantastical world, brimming with vibrant colours, surreal imagery, and a sense of boundless possibility. Through their diverse mediums, which range from painting and mixed media to digital art, Price seamlessly blends elements of the familiar and the otherworldly, creating compositions that captivate and intrigue.

item.title: Sarah Walmsley
item.description: Sandra Walmsley is a renowned sculptor whose work explores themes of memory, absence and presence, loss, and female identity. Through the body language and essence of her sculptures, combined with the mediums in which they are created, Walmsley addresses these profound concepts.Initially focusing on self-portraits, Walmsley's most recent body of work, "By Women, for Women," includes portraits of various female figures. Her work addresses the ways in which the female body has been voyeuristically represented in art and aims to reclaim the female 'nude' and self-portrait through representations of 'naked nudes' and authentic portraits of women, created by a female artist.Walmsley's portraits honour and celebrate the power, strength, and beauty of women, representing their intersectional identities. Exploring the self-portrait as a mode of processing identity, memory, and navigating the process of grieving the loss of mothers and mother-figures, Walmsley's work resonates with viewers on a deeply personal level. Through her captivating sculptures, Walmsley has established herself as a powerful voice in the art world, championing the female experience and reclaiming the narrative around the representation of the female body.

item.title: Sydney Selepe
item.description: Sydney Selepe (b. 1964) is an artist whose creative vision is deeply rooted in his engagement with the world around him. Inspired by his immediate surroundings, as well as the broader socio- economic and political conditions that shape the experiences of individuals and communities, Selepe's art serves as a reflection of the complex and multifaceted realities of contemporary society.In Selepe's artistic practice, the interplay between the tangible and the conceptual is a constant driving force. He draws inspiration from the sights, sounds, and narratives that permeate his daily life, translating these into visually striking compositions that invite the viewer to ponder the nuances of the human condition.

item.title: Thamsanqa Mfuphi
item.description: Thamsanqa Mfuphi presents a powerful series titled "Inkunzi isematholeni," which symbolically conveys that future leaders emerge from today's youth. Inspired by his personal struggles growing up in rural Tsholotsho, Zimbabwe, Mfuphi delves into the challenges faced by South Africans and Africans in general.Through monumental figures and evocative landscapes, he questions the paradoxical situation of being prisoners of our own riches. In this series, Mfuphi employs unconventional materials, such as old prison blankets donated by the Mpumalanga.Correctional services, clothing pegs and a unique combination of cow dung and acrylic paint. The raw nature of these materials serves as a metaphor for struggle, representing individuals born into difficult circumstances, feeling trapped, yet striving to create light and optimism in their lives. Through this thought-provoking body of work, Mfuphi offers a poignant reflection on resilience, transformation, and the indomitable human spirit.

item.title: Thato Kokwana
item.description: As an expressionist glass blower, I embark on a journey of self-discovery and cultural exploration. My work serves as a conduit to reconnect with my cultural identity and delve into the depths of my lineage. Through the intricate use of surnames, clan names, memories, objects, and iconographies, I weave a captivating narrative that reaches back to my ancestral roots.“In the realm of glass, I find a material that resonates with my artistic vision. Its textures provide a grounding force, a tangible connection to the essence of my identity. In a world brimming with vibrant colors and modern influences, I discovered a void within, a yearning for a deeper connection to my origins.”“Through my art, I bridge the gap between the present and the past, infusing my creations with the palpable echoes of home and a constant reminder of where I come from. Each piece becomes a vessel for nostalgia, a testament to the power of art in reconnecting us with our heritage and shaping our sense of self.”

item.title: Thembelihle Ngesi
item.description: Thembelihle Ngesi (b. 1991) is an East London-based fine visual artist whose deeply intuitive practice positions art as an essential spiritual sanctuary. Born in the small rural village of Xhana along the Chalumna River in the Eastern Cape, Ngesi turned to the natural world early in life to navigate childhood health challenges and feelings of isolation. For Ngesi, the canvas operates not merely as a creative outlet, but as a literal home—a transcendental realm where they can experience true solace, vulnerability, and complete freedom from worldly burdens.At the core of Ngesi’s creative evolution is a dedicated practice of Hatha yoga and an obsession with spiritual refinement, which they credit with transforming their mental state and unlocking their creative voice. The pristine geography of the Eastern Cape serves as a powerful wellspring of inspiration, infusing their abstract and figurative paintings with the innate beauty, tranquility, and rhythmic harmony found in the environment

item.title: Victor Geduldt
item.description: State, Geduldt is a entirely self-taught artist who began experimenting with various creative mediums at the age of fourteen. Lacking formal institutional access as a child, he famously honed his visual sensibilities by peering through the windows of commercial art galleries in Bloemfontein, quietly absorbing the techniques of celebrated regional masters such as Frans Claerhout.Working primarily in oils and acrylics, Geduldt acts as his own photographer, documenting his immediate environment to use as direct reference material for his canvas work. His highly textured compositions explore the profound interplay between light and shadow, utilizing a controlled, earthy palette and sharp tonal contrasts to illuminate atmospheric landscapes, pastoral scenes, and the quiet dignity of rural life.Beyond landscapes, Geduldt is an accomplished portraitist dedicated to capturing the raw emotions and facial expressions of individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds. His art deliberately celebrates cultural heritage while confronting socio-economic realities, as seen in poignant works like After School and Loadshedding.

item.title: Zakhele Hlabisa
item.description: Zakhele Hlabisa was born in Mtubatuba North KwaZulu-Natal. Zakhele Hlabisa is an artist whose diverse creative expressions encompass painting, portraits, drawings, and prints. With a profound focus on cultural identity, religion, and political issues, Zakhele Hlabisa's work serves as a powerful exploration of personal and societal narratives.Through his art, Zakhele delves into the intricate layers of his own cultural identity, seeking to understand and celebrate the rich tapestry of his heritage. His creations act as a visual dialogue, inviting viewers to contemplate the complexities of their own cultural backgrounds and the broader human experience. .

item.title: Thulani Gankca
item.description: Thulani Gankca (b. 1993, Welkom, South Africa) is a self-taught, full-time contemporary multidisciplinary artist, professional printmaker, and painter. His work explores themes of culture, identity, and heritage through symbolic use of maize/corn and the imagery of the "suit and tie"—figures he refers to as the "corn people." These recurring motifs form part of a broader inquiry into the social and spiritual narratives rooted in his personal and ancestral history.Raised between Gauteng and Engcobo village in the Eastern Cape, Gankca’s art is deeply informed by his life journey and the duality of urban and rural experiences. His creative practice blends traditional and contemporary techniques, anchored by a strong visual storytelling language.In 2023, he earned a Professional Printmaking Certificate from Artist Proof Studio (APS), where he was awarded the prestigious Ubuntu Award during his second year. His work was also selected for the Presidential Employment Stimulus Programme (PESP4) and commissioned by the National Museum under the mentorship of Christiaan Diedericks in 2024. Gankca holds a Diploma in Human Resources Management (Ekurhuleni West College, 2018) and completed a bridging course in Archives and Records Management through UNISA in 2024. He is currently enrolled to pursue a BA in Visual Multimedia Arts at the University of South Africa in 2025.Gankca has participated in several local and international group exhibitions. His practice continues to evolve as he navigates themes of self-discovery and cultural memory. He lives and works full-time from Ellis House Studios in Johannesburg.

item.title: Abel Bedilu
item.description: Abel Bedilu (b. 2001, Ethiopia) is an Addis Ababa-based contemporary artist working at the innovative intersection of monotype printmaking and experimental street photography. His practice captures the pulse of a rapidly evolving capital, translating the chaotic rhythm of contemporary Ethiopian life into haunting, ethereal visual narratives. Through a unique methodology that blends the mechanical precision of print with the spontaneity of the lens, Bedilu produces blurred, highly dynamic compositions that explore the fluid boundaries of human movement, collective memory, and raw urban energy.His striking imagery frequently reflects deeply personal and societal themes of time, emotional disconnection, and self-reflection within a shifting landscape. By actively embracing chance, texture, and unpredictability in his process, Bedilu allows the physical medium to dictate its own narrative path. The resulting body of work serves as a powerful psychological portrait of a generation caught in suspension—navigating the delicate friction between cultural inertia and relentless modern progress. Through this lens, his art becomes both a witness to urban transformation and an intimate space for existential contemplation.

item.title: Adama Delphine Fawundu
item.description: Adama Delphine Fawundu is a Brooklyn-based visual artist of Mende, Bubi, and Krim ancestry. Her practice engages themes of ancestral technology, intelligence, memory, and radical imagination. She has exhibited internationally, including at the 36th São Paulo Biennial in Brazil, the Congo Biennial (2025), and the inaugural Malta Biennial (2024). Her current solo exhibitions are on view at the Utah Museum of Fine Arts (September 13, 2025 - June 14, 2026) and the Harvey Gantt Center for African American Art & Culture in Charlotte, NC (October 3, 2025 - March 8, 2026)..Fawundu is the co-author of the critically acclaimed book MFON: Women Photographers of the African Diaspora. She is the recipient of numerous honors, including the Guggenheim Fellowship, CatchLight Fellowship, Anonymous Was A Woman Award, and the Rema Hort Mann Artist Grant. Her work is held in the permanent collections of the Brooklyn Museum of Art, Princeton University Art Museum, Newark Museum of Art, Portland Museum of Art, Bryn Mawr College, Norton Museum of Art, and the David C. Driskell Center. She is also an Assistant Professor of Visual Arts at Columbia University.

item.title: Adeleke Femi
item.description: Adeleke Femi (b. 1997) is an powerhouse Nigerian visual artist hailing from Osun State, widely celebrated for his fierce, emotionally charged expressionist painting style. His visceral canvases act as psychological portals, exploring awakened ancestral memories, fragmented nostalgia, and familiar sensory experiences. Rather than merely documenting the physical world, Femi utilizes a highly kinetic, heavily textured brushwork to give explosive voice to the silent internal landscape—mapping personal fears, raw human vulnerabilities, collective aspirations, and surreal dream states.His striking artistic language is backed by a rigorous academic foundation. He earned a National Diploma in Fine Art from the Polytechnic of Ibadan before refining his studio practice at the University of Lagos (UNILAG), where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts. Moving fluidly between oil and acrylic mediums, Femi turns the canvas into a battlefield of vibrant colour and dense impasto texturing to capture the enduring resilience of the contemporary African spirit.A rapidly ascending figure in West Africa's modern art circuit, Femi’s work has garnered widespread institutional attention. His portfolio has been featured in a string of high-profile showcases and curated exhibitions, including the prestigious +234 Art Fair, TotalEnergies Art Exhibition, Emerging Expressions, An Ode to Odd at Madhouse, Brushstrokes of Hope, Boundaries and Bridges at Iriri Art Gallery, and Unbound curated by Creathab. Represented on premier global platforms like Latitudes Online, his paintings reside in significant private collections worldwide, standing as an urgent, unapologetic celebration of emotional honesty and cultural memory.

item.title: Aksah Seyoum
item.description: Aksah Seyoum is a dedicated printmaker with a bachelor's degree in printmaking from Alle University, where she refined her technical skills and broadened her artistic vision. Her work celebrates Ethiopian culture, exploring themes of identity, tradition, and the connection between modern life and ancestral heritage. Aksah's intricate designs and precise techniques bring stories to life, reflecting both personal and collective experiences. She is particularly drawn to scarification patterns, using them as a medium to express her fascination with cultural traditions. Each mark tells a unique story, making her work a meaningful exploration of art, culture, and narrative. . . .

item.title: Alexia Smit
item.description: Dr. Alexia Smit is a highly innovative South African painter, media scholar, and educator whose unique practice operates at the intersection of critical television studies and contemporary visual arts. Holding a PhD in Film and Television Studies from the University of Glasgow, Smit integrates fine art painting directly with rigorous cultural theory. Her research-heavy studio practice treats paint not merely as a creative medium, but as an active analytical tool to investigate, deconstruct, and challenge how the complex social geography of Cape Town is historically represented on South African television screens.By reinterpreting and re-authoring specific scenes from local broadcast dramas, her canvases strip away commercial veneers to reveal deeply rooted spatial and social inequalities. This methodology is brilliantly showcased in her celebrated painting series inspired by the neo-noir local drama Skemerdans.Rejecting the glossy, tourism-driven, and wealth-centered images of the Mother City often broadcast to global audiences, Smit's moody, atmospheric compositions portray a gritty, familiar, and authentic working-class cityscape. Currently serving as a Senior Lecturer in Film and Television Studies at the University of Cape Town (UCT), she actively extends her research beyond traditional text. Smit frequently collaborates with academic colleagues and local artists to produce illustrated zines and public archives on South African visual culture, democratising art theory and making critical media literacy accessible to wider communities.

item.title: Alsadig Mahmoud
item.description: Alsadig Mahmoud (born 1983, Khartoum North, Sudan) is a Sudanese multidisciplinary artist whose work draws deeply from Sudanese culture and symbolism to reflect the experiences of his people both at home and in exile. Blending painting, drawing, collage, and sculpture, he creates visual narratives that explore peace, conflict, humanity, and hope.His compositions often merge architectural forms, figures, and natural elements, capturing a poetic harmony between movement and memory. Mahmoud has exhibited in Transformations: New Perspectives (Nairobi), Nordic Encounters (Stockholm), Anthropology of Detachment (Nairobi), Home: A Daydream (Nairobi), and Echos of Place (Kampala). He currently lives and works in Nairobi, Kenya.

item.title: Amani Azhari
item.description: Amani Azhari Amani Azhari; (b.1998) visual artist from Sudan, received her bachelor's in fine and Applied Arts in 2022 from University of Sudan. and participated in numerous internal exhibitions in her home country. After obtaining her Bachelor's degree in Fine and Applied Arts from the University of Sudan in 2022, she ventured to Kampala, Uganda.Continuing her artistic journey through residencies and exhibitions, she has recently been painting from her studio in Nairobi, Kenya. Amani finds inspiration in girls' sessions, where they express their thoughts and experiences in a society that often silences them with numerous restrictions. Through these sessions, she shares blame, fears, and even beautiful sentiments that are difficult to disclose publicly. Utilizing girls as a fundamental element in her expression, she draws from her personal features to strengthen her message.

item.title: Annette Faul
item.description: Annette Faul is a South African artist based in Stellenbosch, known for her botanical art, maps, and landscape drawings. Her work captures ephemeral moments in nature, with a focus on plants and seasonal transformations.Faul studied Landscape Architecture at the University of Pretoria and the University of Cape Town, and completed a botanical art masterclass with Beverley Allen. Her paintings, such as Bokkeveld in August, celebrate the changing seasons, the interplay of biomes, and the vivid colors of indigenous flora. Through meticulous brushstrokes and detailed observation, she evokes a sense of belonging, awe, and memory in the landscapes of the Western and Northern Cape.

item.title: April Kamunde
item.description: April Kamunde (b. 1988, Nairobi) is an acclaimed Kenyan contemporary painter whose deeply introspective studio practice serves as a tender, luminous space for meditations on rest, womanhood, and collective belonging. Kamunde formalised her visual vocabulary at Kenyatta University, where she graduated with a Bachelor of Education in Fine Art. After spending seventeen years dedicated to meticulous, commercial portrait commissions, a pivotal shift occurred in 2020 when she transitioned into a full-time, independent studio practice. Working primarily in oils on large-scale canvases, Kamunde builds lush, atmospheric compositions where Black women intentionally reclaim softness, time, and emotional presence within a demanding modern world.Her celebrated ongoing series, Rest: The Pursuit of Peace and Fabric of Our Being, transform an ordinary everyday garment—the dera—into a powerful symbol of psychological healing, personal agency, and ancestral power. Originating as a traditional Somali dress that expanded across the East African coast, the loose-fitting cotton dera is re-imagined by Kamunde as a protective armor of comfort that strips away Western capitalist expectations of constant productivity. Through delicate, layered brushwork and rich, vibrant palettes, she paints dreamlike worlds of renewal, framing the act of sleeping or reclining not as luxury, but as an urgent form of quiet resistance.

item.title: Billie Zangewa
item.description: Billie Zangewa (b. 1973, Blantyre, Malawi) is an acclaimed contemporary visual artist who lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. Best known for her intricate, narrative-driven hand-sewn silk collages, Zangewa holds a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Rhodes University in Grahamstown, where she initially specialised in printmaking. After relocating to Johannesburg, she worked briefly in fashion and graphics, an experience that shifted her attention away from the printing press and toward the raw textures of textiles. Her work draws deeply from her own lived experience, using fragments of raw, vibrant silks to explore themes of gender, hidden domestic labour, and systemic racial prejudice.Through delicate, meticulously layered textile compositions, Zangewa portrays intimate, autobiographical scenes of everyday life. Her pieces are frequently centered on her own identity as a mother, partner, and creator, mapping the internal emotional landscape of modern Black womanhood. By elevating mundane domestic tasks into monumental public artworks, Zangewa intentionally transforms the personal into the political. Her figurative works reject the historic objectification of the Black female body, creating instead a safe space for self-representation, quiet empowerment, and soft resilience.Her pioneering approach to fabric art has earned her massive global recognition. Zangewa's works have been featured in major international solo exhibitions, including showcases at the Norval Foundation in Cape Town, the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco, and the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Her striking collages are housed within permanent public collections worldwide, including the Tate Modern in London, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art in Washington, D.C.

item.title: Blen Deresse
item.description: Blen Deresse is an Addis Ababa-based painter exploring psychological tension through atmospheric compositions. Transitioning from fashion to fine arts, her work captures emotional paralysis, balancing gesture and negative space to reveal the fragile line between comfort and constraint. Her paintings serve as mirrors of unspoken struggles, establishing her as a rising voice in contemporary art.Deresse's practice is marked by a restrained yet evocative visual language, where figures often appear suspended between motion and stillness, echoing states of hesitation, withdrawal, or quiet resistance. Her background in fashion continues to inform her sensitivity to form, texture, and the body, translating into paintings that feel both intimate and distanced at once. By allowing negative space to carry as much weight as her figures, she creates compositions that breathe with tension, inviting viewers to sit with discomfort rather than resolve it.Through this delicate interplay, Deresse's work speaks to broader, often unspoken experiences of anxiety, isolation, and emotional restraint, positioning her practice within a growing dialogue on mental and psychological wellbeing in contemporary African art.

item.title: Bubu Ogisi and Mbali Dhlamini
item.description: Bubu Ogisi (b. 1987) and Mbali Dhlamini (b. 1990) are prominent contemporary African multidisciplinary artists and researchers whose individual and collaborative practices explore materiality, decolonization, and indigenous knowledge systems. Working at the intersection of textiles, archival research, and spiritual philosophy, their artistic synergy bridges West and South African histories. Together, their work forms a dynamic material dialogue that reclaims pre-colonial narratives and challenges Eurocentric aesthetic standards across the global contemporary art landscape.Bubu Ogisi, a Lagos-born fibre artist and Creative Director of the wearable art label I AM I S I G O, creates gravity-defying textile installations that transform organic and upcycled fibers into "memory banks". Conversely, South African visual researcher Mbali Dhlamini conducts tactile and discursive investigations into spiritual practices, language, and ancestral landscapes. Her acclaimed work, including her recent explorations at TEDxJohannesburg, reworks colonial imagery and explores the socio-cultural lifecycle of indigenous plants and textiles—most notably the sacred significance of the ancient indigo plant.

item.title: Carine Mansan
item.description: Carine Mansan (b. 1988, born in Côte d’Ivoire) is sculptor and painter who lives and works in Grand Bassam in Ivory Coast. Born to an Ivorian mother and a French father, she grew up lulled by two cultures. In the Ivory Coast, she spent most of her childhood and adolescence before continuing her studies in France and Montreal.After obtaining a diploma in Interior design at the Ecole de Condé in Paris and then at the University of Montreal, she devoted herself entirely to painting and drawing. She began exhibiting her works in Montreal in 2015. Over the years, she has participated in numerous cultural events at other international venues. Her works are in reputable private collections around the world. Today Mansan’s work is about the feminine image; it is figurative, covering sculpture and realist paintings of portraits and everyday life. She is currently our first Ivory Coast Visiting Fellow at the Noldor Residency for the 2021 year.

item.title: Chantal Masinga
item.description: Chantal Masinga is an oil painter whose intuitive practice explores emotion, perception, and the self through layered, meditative processes. Working in monochrome and limited palettes, she focuses on texture, form, and emotional depth to convey subtle internal states and lingering atmospheres.Her featured painting, Breath Between the Clouds, captures a quiet moment of reflection amid life’s chaos, by using dark tones to evoke mental weight and soft pinks to suggest a soothing counterweight of calm, grace, and care. Drawing inspiration from her immediate surroundings, Masinga’s work transforms ordinary, everyday views into transcendent spaces of stillness, introspective discovery, and lasting emotional connection.

item.title: Drew Minter
item.description: Drew Minter is a visual artist and LGBTQIA+ activist whose practice explores identity and belonging through painting and sculpture. Their work maps queer “safe spaces” across the Eastern Cape – sites of authenticity, memory, and community. Using UV curing nail gel, inspired by his mother’s home salon, Minter merges personal history with contemporary queer expression, bringing elements of their childhood sanctuary into new environments.They holds an MA in Fine Art from Nelson Mandela University and has exhibited at the Pretoria Art Museum. Minter was a Sasol New Signatures Top 100 finalist in both 2021 and 2023 and continues to advocate for queer visibility in South African art.

item.title: Eba Morka
item.description: Eba Morka (b. 1999, Ethiopia) is a contemporary printmaker whose practice bridges traditional Ethiopian visual culture with innovative approaches to contemporary printmaking. A graduate of Addis Ababa University's Alle School of Fine Arts and Design, where he completed a Bachelor of Fine Arts in 2025, Morka explores themes of identity, memory, and cultural continuity through layered, richly textured compositions. Drawing inspiration from Ethiopian motifs, symbolism, and material traditions, he combines established printmaking techniques with experimental processes to create works that are both visually intricate and conceptually engaging.His practice reflects on the relationship between personal experience and collective heritage, transforming cultural references into introspective narratives that invite viewers to consider the enduring resonance of history, place, and identity within contemporary life.

item.title: Emmanuel Koto
item.description: Emmanuel Koto (b. 1989, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo) is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice spans photography, video, sculpture, and installation. Working from an embodied, self-taught methodology, his work investigates the politics of perception: how identities are constructed, negotiated, and often confined through the gaze of others. Drawing from the complexities of racial, social, and cultural hybridity, Koto transforms personal and collective experience into visual inquiries that challenge dominant narratives.His early photo series Kin TV, in which he photographed television broadcasts, evolved into a broader research on societal tensions in contemporary Congolese life. A pivotal moment in his trajectory came in 2019 during a creative exchange in Kinshasa, where he began confronting the psychic weight of visibility and difference, an exploration that continues to define his practice.Koto’s work has been exhibited internationally, including: Vantage Point Sharjah 7 (UAE); the Congo Biennale and Lubumbashi Biennale (DRC); Chroniques Urbaines at the Cité de l’Architecture (Paris); and multiple OFF exhibitions of Dak’Art – Biennale of Contemporary African Art (Senegal). His first institutional solo exhibition took place in 2023 at Horner Eck in Bremen, Germany, following a cross-continental residency between Kinshasa and Bremen.He currently lives and works in Kinshasa, continuing to expand a practice rooted in critical reflection, experimentation, and material transformation.

item.title: Fasil Seboka
item.description: Fasil Seboka (b. 2000, Ethiopia) is a contemporary painter based in Addis Ababa whose practice centres on semi-abstract figurative painting. A graduate of Addis Ababa University's Alle School of Fine Arts and Design, where he completed a Bachelor of Fine Arts in 2025, Seboka combines expressive mark-making with layered compositions to investigate themes of memory, identity, and human connection. Working primarily in oil paint, he balances gestural abstraction with recognisable forms, creating emotionally resonant works that reflect both personal experience and broader social narratives.His paintings are characterised by dynamic brushwork, rich textures, and an intuitive approach to colour, inviting viewers to engage with the fluid relationship between figure and space. Through his evolving practice, Seboka explores the complexities of contemporary life, using painting as a means of expressing the emotional and psychological dimensions of the human experience.

item.title: Gina-Rose Bolligello
item.description: Born in Cape Town, South Africa, in 2001, Gina-Rose Bolligello graduated with a BFA from the University of Cape Town’s Michaelis School of Fine Art in 2024. She was awarded both the Simon Gerson Prize and the Director’s Award for her final body of work.Her current practice is centered around hauntology and the colonial histories that surround the Cape, highlighting untold historical narratives as a means to educate audiences and keep the memory and work of colonised people alive. In areas where there is a lack of visual documentation, she uses ‘ghosts’ to narrate and imagine the lives that once were and which are perhaps still present in alternative forms. Her practice explores various media, including photography, video, and printmaking.

item.title: Hauwa Eeyman Mamman
item.description: Hauwa Eeyman Mamman—affectionately known to her followers and peers as "Eeyman"—is an emerging force in Nigeria’s thriving contemporary photography scene. Based in Nigeria, her artistic practice thrives at the distinct intersection of creative image-making and active community engagement. Mamman’s distinct portfolio, heavily featured on her social media channels, offers a poignant look at modern life through a deeply personal lens. She has built a strong reputation not only for her striking visuals but also for her dedication to the craft, frequently participating in portfolio reviews and industry roundtables. By routinely engaging in critical conversations about her art, Mamman continues to refine her unique perspective while contributing to the growth of African photography.

item.title: Itumeleng Mtshali
item.description: Getrude Itumeleng Mtshali (b. 2001, Thabazimbi) is a contemporary South African painter, photographer, and multi-disciplinary artist currently based in Johannesburg. Balancing a technical eye with a deeply personal visual framework, she earned a Higher Certificate in Architectural Technology from Inscape before pivoting completely to visual arts, completing her Fine Arts training at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits). Her layered practice explores themes of identity, heritage, and resilience, serving as a critical vehicle for narrative-building and cultural documentation.Mtshali’s studio practice focuses heavily on Black identity, colourism, spirituality, and the continuous process of self-acceptance. Influenced by prominent contemporary South African artists like Zandile Tshabalala and Jabulani Dhlamini, her work spans painting, mixed media, and documentary portraiture. A major pillar of her recent portfolio reclaims faith as a space for healing, highlighting the complex tensions and beauty born from the cohabitation of Christianity and Blackness. Her figures are typically captured in quiet, introspective moments of interiority, holding a physical and emotional space for stillness and belonging.

item.title: Jacob van Schalkwyk
